Advisory Opinion No. 24-01: Applying the two-year bar to a former State
employee whose proposed employment
would require creating reports for
submission to her former agency and
discussing such reports with her former
agency with the aim of ensuring that her
private sector employer is in compliance
with requirements of its contract with the
former agency.
INTRODUCTION
The following advisory opinion is issued by the New York State Commission on Ethics
and Lobbying in Government (“Commission”), pursuant to Executive Law § 94(7)(c), in response
to an inquiry from [ ], a former employee of the New York Green Bank (“NYGB”), a division
of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (“NYSERDA”). The inquiry
concerns the application of Public Officers Law § 73(8)(a)(i), the two-year bar, to the inquiring
party’s proposed private sector employment on a project that would involve creating and
submitting reports to NYSERDA and discussing such reports with the former agency for the
purpose of ensuring the employer is in compliance with a contract between NYSERDA and their
employer. The Commission and its predecessor agencies have consistently held that the two-year
bar prohibits a former State employee from engaging in communications with their former agency
that are intended to influence the former agency to make a specific decision or take specific action
This includes engaging in discussions with the former agency concerning the means for performing
the requirements of a contract.

2
[ ] has also suggested that the NYGB, rather than NYSERDA, should be deemed her
former agency for post-employment purposes. As discussed below, the Commission finds that the
NYGB is an entity within NYSERDA that is controlled by NYSERDA and has no identity apart
from NYSERDA. Accordingly, and in line with existing precedent, the Commission finds that
NYSERDA is [ ]’s former agency for two-year bar purposes.
The former NYSERDA employee, in presenting their inquiry, has not presented facts,
circumstances or argument that would distinguish this case from the Commission precedent
interpreting and applying the two-year bar on appearing and practicing before one’s former
agency, or that would call for modification or expansion of Commission precedent.
BACKGROUND
[ ] was an employee of New York Green Bank (“NYGB”), a division of NYSERDA,
as an [ ], until [ ] 2024. While with the Department, the employee was responsible
for leading communication and marketing efforts for NYGB’s comprehensive communications
and outreach activity to support internal and external communications, business development
efforts, and industry relationship building. [ ] worked with NYSERDA’s communications
and marketing teams to build awareness of NYGB mission and impact in advancing the state’s
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act; producing communications material,
including press releases, editorials, executive remarks, interview materials and talking points,
social media content, regulatory summaries, and presentation materials to support media relations
efforts; and working with NYSERDA’s marketing team to develop strategies for messaging,
implementation plans, communications schedules, and budgets for all NYGB marketing.
[ ] is now seeking employment as an [ ] with a private company, located in
[ ], which is developing a [ ] project (the “Project”) with NYSERDA. The employee
will be responsible for developing and monitoring internal tracking systems for their employer to
ensure compliance with the Project contract requirements. [ ] reported that they would prepare
reports for NYSERDA’s review and engage in discussions with NYSERDA both before the first
report, and quarterly thereafter, to ensure that the employer satisfies its contractual obligations to
NYSERDA, including addressing any reporting deficiencies identified by NYSERDA.
APPLICABLE LAW
Public Officers Law § 73(8)(a)(i) provides:
No person who has served as a state officer or employee shall within a period of two years
after the termination of such service or employment appear or practice before such state agency or
receive compensation for any services rendered by such former officer or employee on behalf of
any person, firm, corporation, or association in relation to any case, proceeding, application or
other matter before such agency.
DISCUSSION
The post-employment restrictions are intended to prevent former State employees from
“utilizing . . . knowledge, experience and contacts gained in State service to the benefit of a private
Restoring public trust in state government

3
client or to his or her own personal gain.”1 For two years after leaving State service, the two-year
bar generally prohibits former State employees from engaging in activity or communications, or
being paid for rendering services, that are intended to influence a decision or action by their former
agency or to seek from their former agency any information that is not publicly available.2 The
two-year bar contains two discrete provisions – the “appear or practice” clause and the “backroom
services” clause.3
Some examples of activities that have been determined to be prohibited by the appearance
or practice clause are negotiating a contract with a former agency;4 submitting a grant proposal or
application to a former agency;5 representing a client in an audit before a former agency;6 engaging
in settlement discussions with a former agency;7 or calling a former agency to seek guidance on
how it would be likely to apply a regulation in the future, if the agency would not generally provide
such information.8
The backroom services clause of Public Officers Law § 73(8)(a)(i) prohibits a former
employee from providing services for compensation in relation to any case, proceeding or
application, or other matter before the individual’s former agency, even without a personal
appearance before the former agency.9 The backroom services clause specifically prohibits a
former State employee, for example, from accepting compensation to prepare documents for a
private firm when it is reasonably foreseeable that the documents will be reviewed by the
individual’s former agency,10 accepting compensation for assisting another person in the creation
or development of an application to be submitted to the former employee’s State agency, or a plan
or strategy for influencing a decision of the former employee’s State agency.11
The Commission and its predecessor agencies have addressed the specific application of
the two-year bar in the context of performing a contract that involves one’s former agency. The
State Ethics Commission held that “once a contract has been awarded, the contract itself is not a
matter before the agency, and a former employee is not prohibited from working on the contract
merely because his former agency has awarded it.”12 Therefore, the two-year bar permits a former
employee to engage in the performance of a contract involving their former agency. However,

while working on such a contract, a former employee must still take care to avoid violations of the
two-year bar. For example, a former employee is prohibited from engaging in any effort to
influence the agency’s decisions regarding performance of the contract [project] and must not have
reason to seek guidance from the former agency.13 Thus, here, the former employee would be
prohibited from “engaging in technical discussion with the agency to resolve problems in the
field,” if there is disagreement between the agency and the contractor regarding how to resolve
such problems.14
[ ]’s tasks in the proposed post-State employment would appear to fall squarely within
these prohibitions, as they would be generating project reports for NYSERDA and, even more
pointedly, working with NYSERDA to resolve any deficiencies in the employer’s contract
performance. One of the key purposes of the two-year bar - to prevent the creation of the
impression in others that a former State employee may enjoy special treatment when dealing with
former colleagues in their official capacities - is wholly frustrated under such circumstances.15
The inquiring individual has suggested that the NYGB, and not NYSERDA, should be
deemed their former agency for purposes of the two-year bar. However, typically, under the two-
year bar, one’s former agency includes all the constituent units of the agency; application of the
bar is not limited to the division(s) or unit(s) within the agency to which the employee was
assigned.16 Admittedly, there can be an exception to this rule where evidence establishes that the
employing unit is sufficiently separate from the host agency so as to constitute a truly independent
entity.17 No such indicia are present here.
The NYGB has no independent legal status, having been created by an order of the New
York State Public Service Commission, pursuant to a petition filed by NYSERDA, as a division
within NYSERDA.18 The NYGB is led by an Executive Director who reports to NYSERDA’s
President and Chief Executive Officer.19 The NYGB is governed by NYSERDA rules and
oversight, including annual reporting requirements, budget reporting requirements, and
independent audit requirements. The NYGB and its officers and employees are also subject to all
of the statutory requirements and controls that already apply to NYSERDA and its employees,
including, among others, the Public Authorities Law, the Internal Control Act, and the Public
Officers Law, and to oversight by the Authorities Budget Office.20 The NYGB coordinates with
other NYSERDA programs and external public and private entities,21 and [ ] worked with

NYSERDA employees while serving the NYGB. Clearly, the NYGB, as a division of NYSERDA,
is not an independent entity.
As noted in Advisory Opinion No. 18-01, “the two-year bar’s purpose is not to preclude
one from practicing a given trade, profession or occupation, but, rather, to prevent a former
employee from unfairly trading on contacts and information garnered while in State service to
engage in specific conduct that is intended to influence an official decision.”22 A State employee
is not prohibited from all forms of contact with their former agency but is prevented from engaging
in conduct that is intended to influence a decision or action of their former agency. [ ] is free
to help the proposed employer perform its contract with NYSERDA, but such efforts must not
include drafting reports to be submitted to NYSERDA (even if the former employee’s name does
not appear on the report) or engaging or communicating with NYSERDA to resolve issues arising
on the Project or under the contract.
CONCLUSION
The Commission hereby concludes that the inquiring individual’s former agency for two-
year bar purposes was NYSERDA, and the proposed private sector employment, which would
involve the creation and submission of reports to and discussions with NYSERDA, regarding the
contractual compliance of such reports, would violate the two-year bar in Public Officers Law
73(8)(a)(i).
This opinion, until and unless amended or revoked, is binding on the Commission in any
subsequent proceeding concerning the person who requested it and who acted in good faith, unless
material facts were omitted or misstated by the person in the request for opinion or related
supporting documentation.
